title: Local development stack
summary: The local stack is three Compose files layered by ./taskw: compose.dev.yml for infrastructure, compose.app.yml for the Laravel and React services, and compose.devices.yml for the TLS broker and the Go runtime. Ports are the defaults from .env.example. Infrastructure ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only; the web, API and MQTTS ports listen on all interfaces.

boxes.label: Developer
boxes.detail: ./tooling/bootstrap installs the pinned Task binary and creates .env; ./taskw doctor checks tools and ports. deps:up starts compose.dev.yml alone, stack:up adds compose.app.yml, and devices:setup then devices:up adds compose.devices.yml, which is the normal full stack. There is no reset task and the down tasks keep volumes.

boxes.label: Portal and admin
boxes.detail: Each React app is built into an image and served as static files on container port 80. The API address is a build argument (VITE_API_URL), so changing it needs an image rebuild.

boxes.label: Optional overlays
boxes.detail: compose.monitoring.yml (Grafana 3000, Prometheus 9090, Alertmanager 9093, Loki 3100, runbook 9101) is started by tooling/monitoring/local.py. compose.adapters.yml adds adapter-manager, adapter-worker and the webhook receiver (8095) by hand. compose.devices-test.yml is the disposable environment behind ./taskw devices:test, and compose.webhook-verification.yml adds a local webhook sink.

boxes.label: broker-admin
boxes.detail: Built from the runtime image with a different entrypoint. It is the only thing that changes Mosquitto's credentials and ACLs. devices:up ends by running devices:reprovision-broker in the API container, because a new broker volume has no credentials.

boxes.label: API, workers, scheduler
boxes.detail: One image, seven services: api, five workers (automation, webhooks, default, alerts, assistant) and the scheduler. The API container runs pending migrations, then php artisan serve with eight workers on container port 8000. It never seeds; run the seeders once on a new, empty database.

boxes.label: TimescaleDB
boxes.detail: One PostgreSQL database for Laravel's public schema and the runtime's device_runtime schema. An init script enables TimescaleDB on a new volume. The host port defaults to 15432 so it does not collide with a native Postgres.

boxes.label: Mosquitto
boxes.detail: Password-authenticated MQTT over TLS with Dynamic Security, as in a release. A one-shot mqtt-init service creates the security file once and never resets it. Port 8883 listens on all interfaces so hardware on the LAN can connect. The certificate comes from the local CA that devices:setup generates.

boxes.label: Runtime
boxes.detail: The Go data plane. It publishes no host port: the API reaches it at http://runtime:8081 with a shared token, and it calls back to the API's internal device endpoints. Without the devices overlay there is no runtime, so stack:up alone is for UI and API work.

boxes.label: Mailpit
boxes.detail: Captures every email the API and workers send to mailpit:1025 on the internal network. A captured message proves the mail was generated and handed over, not that it would be delivered.

boxes.label: Simulators
boxes.detail: sparkplug_simulator.py publishes an energy meter and an RGB light (and many water meters with --meters) with credentials that php artisan devices:prepare-simulator writes. Vendor simulators publish native payloads for the adapter overlay. Run one publisher per gateway identity.

boxes.label: NATS JetStream
boxes.detail: Only the runtime uses it. Alone, compose.dev.yml publishes the client port 4222 and the monitor port 8222 on localhost. The devices overlay removes both host ports and replaces the command with a config file that bounds the store.

boxes.label: Redis and Node-RED
boxes.detail: compose.dev.yml starts both and deps:smoke checks them, but no application service is configured to use them: sessions and cache are files and queues use the database. Tenant adapter runtimes are separate containers started by adapter-manager, not this stock Node-RED.

steps.text: ./tooling/bootstrap prepares Task and .env. From there every stack is a ./taskw command that layers Compose files.
./taskw deps:up starts compose.dev.yml alone: TimescaleDB, Redis, NATS, Node-RED and Mailpit, for running the API natively.
./taskw stack:up adds compose.app.yml: the API, five workers, the scheduler, portal and admin, all built from source. There is no Go runtime yet.
./taskw devices:setup writes a local CA, a broker certificate and private tokens into a Git-ignored directory. Existing secrets are kept on reruns.
./taskw devices:up adds compose.devices.yml: Mosquitto over TLS, broker-admin and the runtime. This is the full platform.
devices:up finishes by re-applying every connection's credentials and ACLs through broker-admin, since a new broker volume has none.
A simulator on the host connects to the published MQTTS port with prepared credentials and publishes Sparkplug B.
The runtime receives it from the broker inside the Compose network and stores readings in its own schema.
The portal and admin are static builds. Use one hostname, localhost or 127.0.0.1, so the session cookie is shared with the API.
Redis and the stock Node-RED start with the stack, but nothing uses them.
Monitoring, device adapters, the disposable test environment and the webhook sink are separate overlays. If you forget one when rebuilding a service, that service loses the overlay's settings.
